  labs(title = "Managed Money net position (COT)",
       x = NULL, y = "Net contracts") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "4 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma)

# Arrange in a 2x2 grid
gridExtra::grid.arrange(p_precip, p_temp, p_oni, p_cot,
                        ncol = 2,
                        top  = "Climate and speculative variables, 2000–2023")

Among the climate variables, the precipitation index displays a stable seasonal rhythm with no discernible trend, while the temperature index drifts upward noticeably from the mid-2010s, a pattern that will be examined in the stationarity analysis below. The ONI series oscillates around zero as expected, with the 2015–2016 episode standing out as the most pronounced of the period. The COT net position alternates between extended net long and net short episodes, with the most extreme net short positioning occurring around 2018–2019.

2.3 Correlation Analysis

The correlation matrix below is computed over the 2008–2023 sub-period, which is the longest interval for which all variables, including Robusta prices and the COT net position, are simultaneously available. Pearson correlation coefficients are reported, as they are standard for continuous economic and financial series and measure the degree of linear association between variables, consistent with the linear benchmark models estimated in the following section.

The coefficient between two variables \(X\) and \(Y\) is defined as:

\[r_{XY} = \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T}(X_t - \bar{X})(Y_t - \bar{Y})}{\sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^{T}(X_t - \bar{X})^2 \cdot \sum_{t=1}^{T}(Y_t - \bar{Y})^2}}\]

where \(T\) denotes the number of observations, and coefficients range from \(-1\) to \(+1\).

This chunk computes the Pearson correlation matrix across all 16 variables and renders it as a hierarchically clustered heatmap, restricted to the 2008–2023 sub-period so that the matrix reflects a complete and balanced comparison across all variable pairs. na.omit() is applied after the date filter to remove any remaining sporadic missing values before passing the data to cor().

Show code 
# Define the ordered variable list for the correlation matrix.
# The order follows the variable grouping in the dataset table:
# dependent variables first, then spillovers, macroeconomic,
# fundamentals, climate and speculative variables last.
vars_corr <- c("arabica_price", "robusta_price", "sugar_price", "cocoa_price",
               "cpi", "wti", "fed_funds_rate", "dxy",
               "production", "consumption", "exports", "ending_stocks",
               "indice_precip", "indice_temp", "oni", "cot_net_mm")

# Restrict to 2008-2023: the longest window for which all 16
# variables are simultaneously available (Robusta from 2008,
# COT from June 2006 — the binding constraint is Robusta).
# na.omit() removes any remaining sporadic gaps before cor().
df_corr <- dataset_mensuel %>%
  filter(date >= "2008-01") %>%
  select(all_of(vars_corr)) %>%
  na.omit()

# Compute the Pearson correlation matrix on the filtered sample.
# Pearson coefficients measure linear association and are the
# standard choice for continuous economic and financial series.
mat_corr <- cor(df_corr, method = "pearson")

# Replace internal variable names with readable English labels
# for display. The order must match vars_corr exactly.
labels_corr <- c("Arabica", "Robusta", "Sugar", "Cocoa",
                 "CPI", "WTI", "Fed Funds Rate", "DXY",
                 "Production", "Consumption", "Exports", "Ending stocks",
                 "Precipitation", "Temperature", "ONI", "COT net MM")
colnames(mat_corr) <- rownames(mat_corr) <- labels_corr

# Render the correlation heatmap.
# Key display choices:
#   method = "color"  : filled colour tiles (cleaner than circles)
#   type   = "upper"  : show upper triangle only (matrix is symmetric)
#   order  = "hclust" : reorder variables by hierarchical clustering
#                       so that highly correlated groups appear adjacent
#   rev(COL2("RdBu", 200)) : red-to-blue diverging palette where
#                       red = +1, white = 0, and blue = -1.
#                       RdBu's default order runs red (low) to
#                       blue (high), so the palette is reversed
#                       to match the desired convention.
#   addCoef.col       : print correlation coefficients inside each cell
corrplot(mat_corr,
         method      = "color",
         type        = "upper",
         order       = "hclust",
         tl.cex      = 0.72,
         tl.col      = "black",
         addCoef.col = "black",
         number.cex  = 0.52,
         col         = rev(COL2("RdBu", 200)),
         title       = "Pearson correlation matrix — 2008–2023",
         mar         = c(0, 0, 2, 0))

The correlation matrix reveals several patterns of interest. Among the price variables, Arabica and Sugar display the strongest pairwise correlation (0.71), while Arabica and Robusta are moderately correlated (0.67). The most salient feature of the matrix is the high degree of collinearity among the macroeconomic and fundamental variables, as Production, Consumption, Exports and CPI form a tightly correlated cluster with pairwise coefficients ranging from 0.73 to 0.92, reflecting their common upward trends over the period. This multicollinearity motivates the principal component analysis conducted in the following section.

Arabica prices show a moderate negative correlation with Ending Stocks (−0.46) and with the ONI index (−0.36). The correlation between Arabica and the COT net position (0.57) is among the strongest observed between a non-price predictor and a price variable. WTI and DXY display a notable negative correlation (−0.52). Climate variables show relatively weak correlations with prices in levels, with coefficients generally below 0.20 in absolute value.

2.4 Principal Component Analysis

The high degree of collinearity observed in the correlation matrix motivates a principal component analysis of the predictor space. The PCA is conducted purely as a diagnostic tool to quantify the extent of redundancy among the 14 explanatory variables; no principal component is retained as a regressor in the forecasting models.

This chunk runs a principal component analysis on the 14 explanatory variables to quantify the multicollinearity already suggested by the correlation matrix. The PCA is performed on the same 2008–2023 sub-period, with all variables standardised to zero mean and unit variance before decomposition. No component is used downstream in the forecasting models; the analysis is purely diagnostic and serves only to confirm the extent of redundancy in the predictor set.

Show code 
# The two dependent variables (Arabica and Robusta prices) are
# excluded from the PCA: the goal is to characterise the
# structure of the predictor space, not to include targets.
vars_pca <- c("sugar_price", "cocoa_price", "cpi", "wti", "fed_funds_rate",
              "dxy", "production", "consumption", "exports",
              "ending_stocks", "indice_precip", "indice_temp",
              "oni", "cot_net_mm")

labels_pca <- c("Sugar", "Cocoa", "CPI", "WTI", "Fed Funds Rate",
                "DXY", "Production", "Consumption", "Exports",
                "Ending stocks", "Precipitation", "Temperature",
                "ONI", "COT net MM")


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — STANDARDISE THE PREDICTOR MATRIX
# scale() centres each variable to zero mean and scales to
# unit variance. This is mandatory when variables are measured
# in different units (USD/barrel, index points, mm, °C, etc.)
# since PCA is sensitive to the scale of the input variables.
# center = FALSE and scale. = FALSE are passed to prcomp()
# because scaling has already been applied manually, avoiding
# a second standardisation pass.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_pca_data <- dataset_mensuel %>%
  filter(date >= "2008-01") %>%
  select(all_of(vars_pca)) %>%
  na.omit() %>%
  scale()

colnames(df_pca_data) <- labels_pca

# Run PCA on the pre-standardised matrix
pca_result <- prcomp(df_pca_data, center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 2 — COMPUTE VARIANCE EXPLAINED BY COMPONENT
# sdev contains the standard deviation of each component.
# Squaring gives the eigenvalue (variance); dividing by the
# sum of all eigenvalues gives the proportion explained.
# cumsum() accumulates these proportions for the scree plot.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

var_exp <- (pca_result$sdev^2) / sum(pca_result$sdev^2) * 100
var_cum  <- cumsum(var_exp)

df_scree <- data.frame(
  PC         = factor(paste0("PC", 1:length(var_exp)),
                      levels = paste0("PC", 1:length(var_exp))),
  Variance   = var_exp,
  Cumulative = var_cum
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 3 — SCREE PLOT (FIRST 10 COMPONENTS)
# Bars show individual variance explained per component.
# The brown cumulative line traces variance accumulated across
# components. The dashed horizontal line marks the 80%
# threshold. Value labels are added above each bar and on
# the cumulative line points for readability.
# Only the first 10 components are shown since the remaining
# four contribute negligible variance individually.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

p_scree <- ggplot(df_scree[1:10, ], aes(x = PC)) +
  geom_bar(aes(y = Variance), stat = "identity",
           fill = "#2E5090", alpha = 0.8, width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(y = Variance,
                label = paste0(round(Variance, 1), "%")),
            vjust = -0.5, size = 2.8,
            color = "#2E5090", fontface = "bold") +
  geom_line(aes(y = Cumulative, group = 1),
            color = "#8B4513", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(y = Cumulative),
             color = "#8B4513", size = 2.5) +
  geom_text(aes(y = Cumulative,
                label = paste0(round(Cumulative, 1), "%")),
            vjust = -0.8, size = 2.5, color = "#8B4513") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 80, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = 82.5,
           label = "80% threshold", color = "grey40",
           size = 3, hjust = 0) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 110),
                     breaks = seq(0, 100, 20)) +
  labs(title    = "PCA — Variance explained by component",
       subtitle = "Bars: individual variance (%)  |  Brown line: cumulative variance (%)",
       x = NULL, y = "Variance explained (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x        = element_text(size = 10)
  )


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 4 — DISPLAY THE SCREE PLOT
# Only the variance-explained plot is shown; no loading plot
# or component-level interpretation is produced, since no
# principal component is used in the forecasting models that
# follow. The PCA serves solely to confirm, in a single plot,
# the degree of redundancy already suggested by the
# correlation matrix.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

p_scree

The scree plot confirms that the predictor set is genuinely multidimensional, with five components required to cross the conventional 80% threshold. No single factor dominates the variance structure, even though strong pairwise collinearity exists among specific subsets of variables as shown in the correlation matrix above.

2.5 Stationarity Tests

Prior to model estimation, all series are tested for stationarity using two complementary procedures. The Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test evaluates the null hypothesis of a unit root, with rejection at the 5% level indicating stationarity. The KPSS test evaluates the null hypothesis of stationarity, with rejection at the 5% level indicating non-stationarity. A series is classified as stationary when both tests agree, that is, when the ADF rejects its null and the KPSS does not reject its null. This dual-confirmation criterion reduces the risk of misclassification arising from the size distortions of each test individually. Series for which at least one test indicates non-stationarity are re-tested in first differences to determine the appropriate integration order \(d\) prior to inclusion in the ARIMAX and linear regression models.

The chunk below implements this testing procedure for all 15 variables. Series flagged as non-stationary by at least one test are automatically selected for re-testing in first differences, so the second table is generated without manual intervention. Result columns are colour-coded in green for stationary and red for non-stationary, making disagreements between the two tests directly visible.

Show code 
# Variables to test and their display labels.
# The COT net position is excluded here because its 77-month
# gap at the start of the sample would distort the test results;
# its stationarity properties are discussed in the text.
vars_test <- c("arabica_price", "robusta_price", "sugar_price", "cocoa_price",
               "cpi", "wti", "fed_funds_rate", "dxy",
               "production", "consumption", "exports", "ending_stocks",
               "indice_precip", "indice_temp", "oni")

labels_test <- c("Arabica futures", "Robusta futures", "Sugar No.11", "Cocoa NY",
                 "CPI", "WTI", "Fed Funds Rate", "DXY",
                 "Production", "Consumption", "Exports", "Ending stocks",
                 "Precipitation index", "Temperature index", "ONI")


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# TEST FUNCTION — ADF AND KPSS ON A SINGLE SERIES
# Both tests are wrapped in tryCatch() to handle edge cases
# where the series is too short or constant, returning NA
# rather than throwing an error that would halt the pipeline.
#
# Decision rules applied:
#   ADF  : p-value < 0.05 -> reject unit root -> Stationary
#   KPSS : p-value > 0.05 -> fail to reject stationarity -> Stationary
# A series is classified as stationary only when both tests
# agree; conflicting results are resolved by the first-
# difference tests in the second table.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

tester_serie <- function(x) {
  adf  <- tryCatch(adf.test(x, alternative = "stationary"),
                   error = function(e) list(statistic = NA, p.value = NA))
  kpss <- tryCatch(kpss.test(x, null = "Level"),
                   error = function(e) list(statistic = NA, p.value = NA))
  data.frame(
    ADF_stat    = round(as.numeric(adf$statistic),  3),
    ADF_pval    = round(as.numeric(adf$p.value),    3),
    ADF_result  = ifelse(as.numeric(adf$p.value) < 0.05,
                         "Stationary", "Non-stationary"),
    KPSS_stat   = round(as.numeric(kpss$statistic), 3),
    KPSS_pval   = round(as.numeric(kpss$p.value),   3),
    KPSS_result = ifelse(as.numeric(kpss$p.value) > 0.05,
                         "Stationary", "Non-stationary"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# TABLE 1 — TESTS ON SERIES IN LEVELS
# na.omit() is applied within the loop so that each series
# is tested on its maximum available sample, rather than
# restricting all series to the common 2008-2023 window.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

resultats_niveaux <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(vars_test), function(i) {
  x <- na.omit(dataset_mensuel[[vars_test[i]]])
  if (length(x) == 0) return(NULL)
  cbind(data.frame(Variable = labels_test[i], stringsAsFactors = FALSE),
        tester_serie(x))
}))


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# TABLE 2 — TESTS ON FIRST-DIFFERENCED SERIES
# Only series flagged as non-stationary by at least one test
# in levels are re-tested in differences. The index of those
# series is identified automatically from the level results,
# so this selection updates without manual intervention if
# the variable list changes.
# diff() computes the first difference: x(t) - x(t-1).
# na.omit() is reapplied after differencing to remove the
# leading NA introduced by the lag operation.
# The Unicode prefix Δ (U+0394) is prepended to variable
# names to make clear that first differences are being shown.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

vars_nonstatio_idx <- which(
  resultats_niveaux$ADF_result  == "Non-stationary" |
  resultats_niveaux$KPSS_result == "Non-stationary"
)

resultats_diff <- do.call(rbind, lapply(vars_nonstatio_idx, function(i) {
  x <- na.omit(diff(na.omit(dataset_mensuel[[vars_test[i]]])))
  if (length(x) == 0) return(NULL)
  cbind(data.frame(Variable = paste0("\u0394 ", labels_test[i]),
                   stringsAsFactors = FALSE),
        tester_serie(x))
}))


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# DISPLAY — COLOUR-CODED RESULT COLUMNS
# The ADF result column (col 4) and KPSS result column (col 7)
# are coloured green for Stationary and red for Non-stationary,
# making it immediately visible where tests agree or conflict.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

kable(resultats_niveaux,
      caption   = "ADF and KPSS stationarity tests — series in levels (2000–2023)",
      booktabs  = TRUE,
      col.names = c("Variable", "ADF stat", "ADF p-val", "ADF result",
                    "KPSS stat", "KPSS p-val", "KPSS result")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                font_size = 10, full_width = TRUE) %>%
  column_spec(4, color = ifelse(resultats_niveaux$ADF_result == "Stationary",
                                "darkgreen", "red")) %>%
  column_spec(7, color = ifelse(resultats_niveaux$KPSS_result == "Stationary",
                                "darkgreen", "red"))

Show code 
kable(resultats_diff,
      caption   = "ADF and KPSS stationarity tests — first-differenced series",
      booktabs  = TRUE,
      col.names = c("Variable", "ADF stat", "ADF p-val", "ADF result",
                    "KPSS stat", "KPSS p-val", "KPSS result")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                font_size = 10, full_width = TRUE) %>%
  column_spec(4, color = ifelse(resultats_diff$ADF_result == "Stationary",
                                "darkgreen", "red")) %>%
  column_spec(7, color = ifelse(resultats_diff$KPSS_result == "Stationary",
                                "darkgreen", "red"))

The results from the two stationarity tests are largely consistent and confirm the expected properties of the series. In levels, the majority of variables are non-stationary according to at least one of the two tests. The two dependent variables present contrasting patterns: Arabica futures prices are classified as non-stationary by both tests, confirming the presence of a unit root, while Robusta futures prices yield conflicting results, with the ADF failing to reject the unit root null and the KPSS failing to reject stationarity.

Several additional series present conflicting results in levels. Production and Consumption are stationary according to the ADF but non-stationary according to the KPSS, while Robusta futures and Ending stocks show the reverse pattern. Temperature presents the same conflict as Production and Consumption. In such ambiguous cases, the first-differenced results are decisive.

The second table confirms that a single round of differencing is sufficient to achieve stationarity for all 13 non-stationary or conflicted series: every variable in first differences is classified as stationary by both the ADF and KPSS tests simultaneously. This establishes \(d=1\) as the appropriate integration order for the non-stationary series, the treatment of which varies across model families as discussed in the methodology. The two variables classified as stationary in levels by both tests, namely the precipitation index and the ONI, will be included without transformation.

2.6 Seasonality Analysis

The seasonality analysis examines whether coffee futures prices exhibit systematic within-year patterns that repeat across calendar months. Detecting such patterns is relevant for model specification: if prices follow predictable seasonal cycles, they would need to be accounted for explicitly in the ARIMAX framework through seasonal differencing or seasonal AR/MA components.

The chunk below implements this analysis for both series. Robusta rows prior to 2008 are filtered out before grouping so that monthly averages reflect only the years for which data are available. The ±1 standard deviation ribbon around each monthly mean provides a visual gauge of interannual dispersion: a narrow band relative to the cross-month range signals consistent seasonality, while a wide band indicates that year-to-year variation dominates any calendar-month pattern.

Show code 
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ARABICA SEASONALITY (2000-2023)
# The month number is extracted from the YYYY-MM date string
# and converted to an ordered factor using month.abb to ensure
# the x-axis displays Jan through Dec in calendar order rather
# than alphabetical order. na.rm = TRUE handles the negligible
# number of missing values without dropping entire months.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_sais_arabica <- dataset_mensuel %>%
  mutate(mois     = as.integer(substr(date, 6, 7)),
         nom_mois = factor(month.abb[mois], levels = month.abb)) %>%
  group_by(mois, nom_mois) %>%
  summarise(moy = mean(arabica_price, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd  = sd(arabica_price,   na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ROBUSTA SEASONALITY (2008-2023)
# Rows with missing Robusta prices (2000-2007) are filtered
# out before grouping so that the cross-year averages reflect
# only the 16 years for which data are available.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_sais_robusta <- dataset_mensuel %>%
  filter(!is.na(robusta_price)) %>%
  mutate(mois     = as.integer(substr(date, 6, 7)),
         nom_mois = factor(month.abb[mois], levels = month.abb)) %>%
  group_by(mois, nom_mois) %>%
  summarise(moy = mean(robusta_price, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd  = sd(robusta_price,   na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PLOTS — SEASONAL PROFILE WITH ±1 SD BAND
# geom_ribbon draws the uncertainty band before geom_line
# so the line is rendered on top of the shaded area.
# group = 1 is required in aes() to connect points across
# the discrete x-axis (nom_mois is a factor, not numeric).
# ----------------------------------------------------------

p_sais_arabica <- ggplot(df_sais_arabica,
                          aes(x = nom_mois, y = moy, group = 1)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = moy - sd, ymax = moy + sd),
              fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(color = "#8B4513", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "#8B4513", size = 2) +
  labs(title    = "Arabica price seasonality — monthly average (2000–2023)",
       subtitle = "Band = ±1 standard deviation. Source: Refinitiv/CEDIF.",
       x = NULL, y = "Average price (USD/lb)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

p_sais_robusta <- ggplot(df_sais_robusta,
                          aes(x = nom_mois, y = moy, group = 1)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = moy - sd, ymax = moy + sd),
              fill = "lightgreen", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(color = "#2E8B57", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "#2E8B57", size = 2) +
  labs(title    = "Robusta price seasonality — monthly average (2008–2023)",
       subtitle = "Band = ±1 standard deviation. Source: Refinitiv/CEDIF.",
       x = NULL, y = "Average price (USD/tonne)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

gridExtra::grid.arrange(p_sais_arabica, p_sais_robusta, ncol = 1)

Both series display weak seasonal patterns across the calendar year. Arabica prices show virtually no systematic monthly variation, with the cross-month range of average prices spanning less than USD 0.05/lb, a negligible amplitude relative to the overall price variability captured by the wide confidence bands. This finding is consistent with the global nature of the Arabica futures market, where prices are driven primarily by supply shocks, macroeconomic conditions and speculative positioning rather than predictable seasonal cycles.

Robusta prices exhibit a slightly more pronounced seasonal profile, with averages rising gradually from January through August before declining toward year-end. However, the amplitude of this seasonal variation remains small relative to the interannual volatility captured by the standard deviation bands, suggesting that seasonality is not a dominant driver of Robusta price dynamics either.

Overall, the absence of strong seasonality in both series is an important finding for the modelling phase: it implies that seasonal differencing or seasonal ARIMA components are unlikely to be necessary, and that the main sources of price variation are structural and cyclical rather than calendar-driven.

3 Methodology

3.1 Model Overview and Estimation Strategy

This study estimates six forecasting models for each of the two dependent variables — Arabica and Robusta futures prices. Two econometric models serve as interpretable benchmarks: an ARIMAX and a multiple linear regression (MLR). Four machine learning models are estimated alongside: Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Machine (SVM) and Artificial Neural Network (ANN). All models are estimated separately for Arabica and Robusta, reflecting the distinct market structures and price determinants of the two varieties.

The monthly dataset covering January 2000 to December 2023 is used for all models except those involving Robusta prices or the COT net position, which are estimated on the restricted sub-periods for which these variables are available. All models are evaluated on the basis of three performance metrics: the coefficient of determination (\(R^2\)), the Mean Squared Error (MSE) and the Mean Absolute Error (MAE).

3.2 Data Preprocessing and Stationarity Handling

The stationarity analysis conducted in the preceding section established that the majority of series are integrated of order one, that is, \(d=1\). For the ARIMAX model, non-stationarity is handled internally by auto.arima(), which selects the appropriate differencing order \(d\) at each estimation step. For the MLR and ML models, all variables are included in levels for the reasons discussed in the following paragraph. The two variables classified as stationary in levels, namely the precipitation index and the ONI, are included without transformation across all model specifications.

For the machine learning models, which impose no distributional assumptions on the input series, all variables are included in their original levels. All variables are normalised to the \([0,1]\) range using Min-Max scaling prior to ML model estimation :

\[x_{\text{scaled}} = \frac{x - x_{\min}}{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}\]

Missing values, arising from the Robusta data gap (2000–2007) and the COT availability constraint (2000–June 2006), are handled by restricting the estimation sample to the sub-period for which all required variables are simultaneously available.

A note on the treatment of non-stationary series in the machine learning models is warranted. While the ARIMAX model handles non-stationarity internally through the differencing parameter \(d\) selected by auto.arima(), the ML models are estimated on the original levels of all series. This choice is deliberate: estimating ML models on first-differenced series, which represent monthly price changes rather than price levels, yielded near-zero \(R^2\) values, confirming that month-to-month price variations are largely unpredictable at this frequency. Estimating on levels allows the ML models to exploit the trending co-movement among variables that carries genuine predictive information about the price trajectory, at the cost of a potential spurious regression concern. This trade-off is acknowledged as a limitation of the study and is discussed further in the limitations section.

3.3 Walk-Forward Validation Protocol

All models are evaluated using a walk-forward (expanding window) validation protocol, which avoids the data leakage that would arise from random cross-validation in a time series context. The dataset is split into a training set comprising the first 80% of observations and a test set comprising the remaining 20%, yielding 168 training observations and 43 test observations for the Arabica sample, and 153 training and 39 test observations for the Robusta sample.

The walk-forward procedure expands the training window by one observation at each step, re-estimates the model, and generates a one-step-ahead forecast. Performance metrics are computed on the out-of-sample forecasts accumulated over the full test period: \(R^2\) measures the proportion of variance in observed prices explained by the forecasts, MSE penalises large errors through quadratic weighting, and MAE reports the average absolute deviation between forecasts and observed values.

The chunk below sets up the shared infrastructure used by all six model chunks: the exogenous variable list, the Min-Max scaling and performance metric functions, and the two dataset variants in levels for Arabica and Robusta separately. The 80/20 split indices are computed once here and passed directly to each model chunk, guaranteeing an identical train/test partition across all estimations.

Show code 
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# EXOGENOUS VARIABLE LIST
# These 14 predictors are passed as regressors to all six
# models. The list is defined once here so that any future
# change to the variable set propagates automatically to
# every model chunk without manual editing.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

vars_exo <- c("sugar_price", "cocoa_price", "cpi", "wti", "fed_funds_rate",
              "dxy", "production", "consumption", "exports",
              "ending_stocks", "indice_precip", "indice_temp", "oni",
              "cot_net_mm")


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# MIN-MAX SCALING FUNCTION
# Rescales a numeric vector to the [0, 1] interval using the
# observed minimum and maximum of that vector. Applied to all
# variables before ML model estimation to ensure that no
# single variable dominates the objective function due to
# its measurement scale. The scaling parameters are derived
# from the full available sample for each variable, not from
# the training set alone — a deliberate simplification noted
# as a minor limitation in the methodology section.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

minmax_scale <- function(x) {
  (x - min(x, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(x, na.rm = TRUE) - min(x, na.rm = TRUE))
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PERFORMANCE METRICS FUNCTION
# Computes R², MSE and MAE on paired vectors of observed and
# predicted values. complete.cases() drops any NA pairs
# before computation, which can arise at the first step of
# the walk-forward loop when the predicted vector has not yet
# been fully populated.
#
# R²  = 1 - SS_res / SS_tot  (proportion of variance explained)
# MSE = mean squared error    (penalises large errors heavily)
# MAE = mean absolute error   (more robust to outliers than MSE)
# ----------------------------------------------------------

calculer_metriques <- function(actual, predicted) {
  ok   <- complete.cases(actual, predicted)
  act  <- actual[ok]
  pred <- predicted[ok]
  data.frame(
    R2  = round(1 - sum((act - pred)^2) / sum((act - mean(act))^2), 4),
    MSE = round(mean((act - pred)^2), 4),
    MAE = round(mean(abs(act - pred)), 4)
  )
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# DATASET PREPARATION FUNCTIONS
# Two functions produce the dataset variants required by
# different model families:
#
# preparer_niveaux() — levels dataset for ARIMAX and MLR.
#   Retains only complete cases (rows where all variables are
#   observed), which restricts the Arabica sample to the
#   post-June 2006 period when COT data become available.
#   auto.arima() handles non-stationarity internally by
#   selecting the differencing order d at each walk-forward
#   step, so no manual differencing is applied here.
#
# preparer_diff() — first-differenced dataset for ML models.
#   Non-stationary variables are differenced once; stationary
#   variables (indice_precip, oni) are left in levels.
#   The leading NA introduced by diff() is removed by the
#   final filter(complete.cases(.)) call.
#   Note: estimating ML models on levels rather than
#   differences was ultimately preferred (see methodology);
#   this differenced dataset is retained for robustness
#   checks but not used in the main results.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

preparer_niveaux <- function(df, var_dep) {
  df %>%
    select(date, all_of(c(var_dep, vars_exo))) %>%
    filter(complete.cases(.)) %>%
    arrange(date)
}

preparer_diff <- function(df, var_dep) {
  # Variables classified as non-stationary in levels (see stationarity chunk)
  vars_to_diff <- c(var_dep, "sugar_price", "cocoa_price", "cpi", "wti",
                    "fed_funds_rate", "dxy", "production", "consumption",
                    "exports", "ending_stocks", "indice_temp")
  df %>%
    select(date, all_of(c(var_dep, vars_exo))) %>%
    filter(complete.cases(.)) %>%
    arrange(date) %>%
    # diff() each non-stationary variable; intersect() ensures only columns
    # present in the dataset are differenced (guards against name mismatches)
    mutate(across(all_of(intersect(vars_to_diff, colnames(.))),
                  ~ c(NA, diff(.x)))) %>%
    filter(complete.cases(.))   # Remove the leading NA row from differencing
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# APPLY PREPARATION FUNCTIONS
# For Robusta, the monthly dataset is pre-filtered to remove
# the 2000-2007 rows before passing to the function, so that
# complete.cases() does not erroneously drop all rows due to
# the structural NA block in robusta_price.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_arabica_levels <- preparer_niveaux(dataset_mensuel, "arabica_price")
df_arabica_diff   <- preparer_diff(dataset_mensuel, "arabica_price")

df_robusta_levels <- preparer_niveaux(
  dataset_mensuel %>% filter(!is.na(robusta_price)), "robusta_price")
df_robusta_diff   <- preparer_diff(
  dataset_mensuel %>% filter(!is.na(robusta_price)), "robusta_price")


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# 80/20 TRAIN/TEST SPLIT
# The split index is the floor of 80% of the available rows
# in each dataset variant. Using floor() ensures the training
# set never accidentally includes a test observation when the
# sample size is not divisible by 5.
# All six model chunks use these indices directly, guaranteeing
# an identical partition across every model and series.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

split_ratio <- 0.80

n_train_ara_lev <- floor(nrow(df_arabica_levels) * split_ratio)
n_train_rob_lev <- floor(nrow(df_robusta_levels) * split_ratio)
n_train_ara_dif <- floor(nrow(df_arabica_diff)   * split_ratio)
n_train_rob_dif <- floor(nrow(df_robusta_diff)   * split_ratio)

# Print sample sizes for verification
cat("Arabica levels — Train:", n_train_ara_lev,
    "| Test:", nrow(df_arabica_levels) - n_train_ara_lev, "\n")
Arabica levels — Train: 168 | Test: 43
Show code 
cat("Robusta levels — Train:", n_train_rob_lev,
    "| Test:", nrow(df_robusta_levels) - n_train_rob_lev, "\n")
Robusta levels — Train: 153 | Test: 39
Show code 
cat("Arabica diff   — Train:", n_train_ara_dif,
    "| Test:", nrow(df_arabica_diff)   - n_train_ara_dif, "\n")
Arabica diff   — Train: 168 | Test: 42
Show code 
cat("Robusta diff   — Train:", n_train_rob_dif,
    "| Test:", nrow(df_robusta_diff)   - n_train_rob_dif, "\n")

4 Results

The following sections report the out-of-sample forecasting results for each of the six models, estimated separately for Arabica and Robusta.

4.1 Multiple Linear Regression (MLR)

This chunk estimates the Multiple Linear Regression benchmark using the same walk-forward expanding window protocol as all other models. Unlike ARIMAX, OLS does not handle non-stationarity internally, so the model is estimated on the levels dataset with the understanding that any spurious regression concern is acknowledged as a limitation. At each step, the entire expanded training window is refitted from scratch using lm(), and a one-step-ahead prediction is generated for the current test observation. The code below is written as a sequence of explicit, separate steps rather than as a single chained pipeline, so that each operation can be inspected individually.

Show code 
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# MLR ESTIMATION FUNCTION
#
# Arguments:
#   df      : levels dataset (one row per month)
#   var_dep : name of the dependent variable column
#             ("arabica_price" or "robusta_price")
#   n_train : size of the initial training window (number of
#             rows), computed earlier in the preprocessing chunk
#
# What the function returns:
#   actual    : the observed prices in the test period
#   predicted : the walk-forward one-step-ahead forecasts
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_mlr <- function(df, var_dep, n_train) {

  # STEP 1 — Keep only the columns this model actually needs:
  # the dependent variable plus the 14 exogenous predictors.
  # vars_exo is defined once in the preprocessing chunk and
  # reused identically by all six models.
  # The intersect() call is a safety check: if a predictor were
  # ever missing from df, it is simply skipped here instead of
  # making the function crash. No complete.cases() check is
  # needed here: df has already been filtered to complete cases
  # by preparer_niveaux() before reaching this function.
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df))
  vars_a_garder <- c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)
  df_modele <- df[, vars_a_garder]

  # STEP 2 — Split into the initial training set and the test
  # set, using the row count computed in the preprocessing
  # chunk (80% / 20% split).
  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele)
  donnees_train <- df_modele[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  # STEP 3 — Walk-forward loop.
  # At forecasting step i, the model is re-estimated using
  # ALL observations available up to that point: the initial
  # training set, plus every test-period row already passed
  # (rows 1 to i-1 of donnees_test). The freshly estimated
  # model is then used to predict row i of the test set, and
  # only that single one-step-ahead prediction is kept.
  #
  # nb_lignes_test_vues starts at 0 (nothing seen yet before
  # the first forecast) and grows by one at every step.
  predictions <- numeric(n_test)   # empty vector to fill in

  for (i in 1:n_test) {

    nb_lignes_test_vues <- i - 1   # 0 at step 1, 1 at step 2, ...

    # Rows of the test set already "seen" before step i.
    # When nb_lignes_test_vues = 0, this selects zero rows,
    # which rbind() below simply ignores.
    lignes_test_vues <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]

    # The expanding training window for this step
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)

    # Re-estimate the linear regression from scratch on the
    # current window. The formula "var_dep ~ ." means: use
    # every other column in the data frame as a predictor.
    formule    <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ ."))
    modele_ols <- lm(formule, data = fenetre_entrainement)

    # Predict the single next observation (row i of the test set)
    ligne_a_predire <- donnees_test[i, ]
    predictions[i]  <- predict(modele_ols, newdata = ligne_a_predire)
  }

  # STEP 4 — Return the observed and predicted test values
  valeurs_observees <- donnees_test[[var_dep]]
  list(actual = valeurs_observees, predicted = predictions)
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ESTIMATION — ARABICA AND ROBUSTA
# ----------------------------------------------------------

res_mlr_ara <- fit_mlr(df_arabica_levels, "arabica_price", n_train_ara_lev)
res_mlr_rob <- fit_mlr(df_robusta_levels, "robusta_price", n_train_rob_lev)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PERFORMANCE METRICS
# Stored in the same standardised format as the other five
# models for direct combination in the comparative performance
# chunk later in this document.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

metriques_mlr <- rbind(
  cbind(Model = "MLR", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_mlr_ara$actual, res_mlr_ara$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "MLR", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_mlr_rob$actual, res_mlr_rob$predicted))
)

The MLR benchmark performs well for Arabica (\(R^2\) = 0.784), capturing a large share of the variance through the linear combination of exogenous variables. For Robusta, however, performance deteriorates significantly (\(R^2\) = 0.276), with an MSE of 114,285 and an MAE of 274.6 USD/tonne. This sharp contrast likely reflects the shorter estimation window available for Robusta (2008–2023), which reduces the number of training observations and amplifies the sensitivity of the OLS estimator to multicollinearity among the predictors, a problem already documented in the correlation and PCA analyses. The MLR results confirm that a purely static linear specification without temporal dynamics is insufficient to model Robusta price dynamics over a restricted sample.

Beyond forecasting accuracy, examining the individual coefficients of the MLR model provides a useful window into the direction and magnitude of each predictor’s estimated effect on coffee prices. The table below reports the OLS estimates from the full training window for each variety, alongside the sign that economic theory would predict for each variable. Inconsistencies between the two are highlighted in red and warrant careful interpretation, as they may reflect genuine sign reversals driven by multicollinearity rather than a failure of the underlying economic reasoning.

This chunk fits an OLS model on the full initial training window for each coffee variety and extracts the regression coefficients using broom::tidy(). The intercept is excluded from the display since it carries no economic interpretation in a levels regression where all variables are trending. For each predictor, the theoretically expected sign is derived from economic reasoning and compared against the observed sign of the estimated coefficient. Rows where the two disagree are highlighted with a light red background to draw immediate attention to potential multicollinearity-driven sign reversals. The Consistent column is coloured green for agreement, red for disagreement, and grey for predictors whose expected sign is theoretically ambiguous.

Show code 
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# MLR COEFFICIENT TABLE WITH EXPECTED VS OBSERVED SIGNS
# The walk-forward MLR results reported above describe
# forecasting accuracy but say nothing about the direction
# or magnitude of individual predictor effects. This chunk
# extracts the OLS coefficients from a model estimated on
# the full initial training window for each series, augments
# them with theoretically expected signs derived from
# economic reasoning, and flags any sign disagreement for
# discussion.
#
# Expected signs:
#   sugar_price    (+) : land substitution in Brazil drives
#                        coffee and sugar prices together
#   cocoa_price    (+) : correlated tropical commodity cycle
#   cpi            (+) : general inflation lifts all nominal
#                        commodity prices
#   wti            (+) : energy costs embedded in production
#                        and transportation
#   fed_funds_rate (-) : tighter monetary policy strengthens
#                        the dollar and reduces risk appetite,
#                        depressing commodity prices
#   dxy            (-) : stronger dollar makes USD-denominated
#                        commodities more expensive for non-US
#                        buyers, reducing demand
#   production     (-) : higher supply pushes prices down
#   consumption    (+) : higher demand pushes prices up
#   exports        (-) : higher exports reduce domestic/global
#                        availability, ambiguous in practice
#   ending_stocks  (-) : larger inventories signal oversupply
#   indice_precip  (-) : excess rainfall can damage cherries
#                        and reduce quality, but moderate
#                        precipitation supports yields —
#                        sign is ambiguous ex ante
#   indice_temp    (-) : above-optimal temperatures reduce
#                        yields, particularly for Arabica
#   oni            (-) : El Niño episodes are associated with
#                        drought in key producing regions,
#                        reducing supply and pushing prices up;
#                        however the index is positive during
#                        El Niño, implying a negative sign
#                        between ONI and price if the supply
#                        channel dominates
#   cot_net_mm     (+) : net long positioning by speculative
#                        funds reflects and amplifies bullish
#                        price expectations
# ----------------------------------------------------------

library(broom)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# DISPLAY LABELS AND EXPECTED SIGNS
# Both vectors follow the same order as vars_exo to ensure
# correct alignment when building the display data frame.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

labels_mlr <- c(
  "sugar_price"    = "Sugar",
  "cocoa_price"    = "Cocoa",
  "cpi"            = "CPI",
  "wti"            = "WTI",
  "fed_funds_rate" = "Fed Funds Rate",
  "dxy"            = "DXY",
  "production"     = "Production",
  "consumption"    = "Consumption",
  "exports"        = "Exports",
  "ending_stocks"  = "Ending stocks",
  "indice_precip"  = "Precipitation",
  "indice_temp"    = "Temperature",
  "oni"            = "ONI",
  "cot_net_mm"     = "COT net MM"
)

signes_attendus <- c(
  "sugar_price"    = "+",
  "cocoa_price"    = "+",
  "cpi"            = "+",
  "wti"            = "+",
  "fed_funds_rate" = "-",
  "dxy"            = "-",
  "production"     = "-",
  "consumption"    = "+",
  "exports"        = "-",
  "ending_stocks"  = "-",
  "indice_precip"  = "?",
  "indice_temp"    = "-",
  "oni"            = "-",
  "cot_net_mm"     = "+"
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# REUSABLE COEFFICIENT EXTRACTION FUNCTION
# Fits an OLS model on the initial training window, extracts
# tidy coefficients via broom::tidy(), drops the intercept
# (not economically interpretable in a levels regression
# with trending variables), recodes variable names to display
# labels, appends expected signs, and flags disagreements.
#
# Arguments:
#   df_levels      : levels dataset (complete cases only)
#   var_dep        : name of the dependent variable column
#   n_train        : size of the initial training window
#   couleur_header : hex colour for the table header row
#   caption_text   : caption string passed to kable()
# ----------------------------------------------------------

extraire_coefs_mlr <- function(df_levels, var_dep, n_train,
                                couleur_header, caption_text) {

  # Fit OLS on the initial training window, same specification
  # as the walk-forward loop in the mlr chunk above.
  modele_lm <- lm(
    as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ .")),
    data = df_levels[1:n_train, c(var_dep, vars_exo)]
  )

  # Extract tidy coefficients: estimate, std error, t-stat, p-value.
  # The intercept is dropped since it carries no economic interpretation
  # in a levels regression where all variables are trending.
  df_coef <- tidy(modele_lm) %>%
    filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
    mutate(
      # Recode internal variable names to display labels
      Variable      = labels_mlr[term],
      # Observed sign derived from the coefficient estimate
      Sign_observed = ifelse(estimate > 0, "+", "-"),
      # Expected sign from economic theory
      Sign_expected = signes_attendus[term],
      # Flag disagreements between observed and expected signs.
      # Ambiguous predictors (marked "?") are never flagged.
      Consistent    = case_when(
        Sign_expected == "?"              ~ "—",
        Sign_observed == Sign_expected    ~ "Yes",
        TRUE                              ~ "No"
      ),
      # Significance stars following conventional thresholds
      Sig = case_when(
        p.value < 0.001 ~ "***",
        p.value < 0.01  ~ "**",
        p.value < 0.05  ~ "*",
        p.value < 0.1   ~ ".",
        TRUE            ~ ""
      )
    ) %>%
    select(Variable, estimate, std.error, statistic,
           p.value, Sig, Sign_expected, Sign_observed, Consistent)

  # Colour the Consistent column: green for agreement,
  # red for disagreement, grey for ambiguous predictors.
  consistent_colors <- ifelse(df_coef$Consistent == "Yes", "#27ae60",
                       ifelse(df_coef$Consistent == "No",  "#c0392b",
                                                           "grey50"))

  kable(df_coef,
        caption   = caption_text,
        booktabs  = TRUE,
        row.names = FALSE,
        digits    = 4,
        col.names = c("Variable", "Estimate", "Std. Error",
                      "t-stat", "p-value", "",
                      "Expected sign", "Observed sign", "Consistent")) %>%
    kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                  font_size = 11, full_width = TRUE) %>%
    # Highlight rows where sign is inconsistent with theory
    row_spec(which(df_coef$Consistent == "No"),
             background = "#fff5f5") %>%
    # Colour the Consistent column
    column_spec(9,
                bold  = df_coef$Consistent != "—",
                color = consistent_colors) %>%
    row_spec(0, bold = TRUE,
             background = couleur_header, color = "white")
}

)

Before diving into the results, it is worth spelling out what sign each predictor is expected to carry and why. Some of these are straightforward, others less so.

Sugar and Cocoa are both expected to carry a positive sign, as they share common market dynamics with coffee through the tropical commodity cycle and, in the case of Sugar, through direct land competition in Brazil. CPI is expected positive because rising general price levels tend to lift all nominal commodity prices along with them. WTI is expected positive because energy costs are embedded in every stage of coffee production and transportation, from fertilisers to freight. The Federal Funds Rate is expected negative because tighter monetary policy strengthens the dollar and reduces risk appetite, both of which tend to weigh on commodity prices. DXY carries the same expected negative sign for a more direct reason: since coffee futures are priced in US dollars, a stronger dollar makes them more expensive for buyers operating in other currencies, which dampens global demand. Production and Ending stocks are both expected negative, as higher supply and larger inventories signal an oversupplied market. Consumption is expected positive as stronger demand pushes prices up. Exports are assigned a negative expected sign as a working assumption, though the theoretical direction is genuinely ambiguous. The ONI index is expected negative because El Niño episodes, which correspond to positive ONI values, are associated with drought in key producing regions and therefore with supply shortfalls that push prices up. COT net MM is expected positive because a larger net long position among speculative funds both reflects and amplifies bullish market expectations. Precipitation is the only variable left without an expected sign, since both excess rainfall and drought can damage coffee yields depending on the timing and severity of the anomaly, making any prior direction difficult to justify.

It is worth noting that the expected signs above reflect the present study’s own reading of the theory. For some variables, a case could reasonably be made for the opposite sign depending on which transmission channel one thinks dominates.

The Arabica results are largely encouraging. COT net MM stands out as the strongest predictor, with a t-statistic of 6.13 and a positive sign fully consistent with theory, confirming that speculative positioning is not just a financial sideshow but a genuine driver of Arabica prices even in a simple linear framework. Sugar and WTI follow closely, both positive and highly significant, which lines up well with the energy cost channel and the Brazil land substitution story. Ending stocks comes in negative and significant, exactly as inventory theory would predict. The remaining variables are individually insignificant, which at this point is no longer surprising given what the VIF table showed us. The two sign inconsistencies, CPI and Production, are both insignificant and almost certainly reflect multicollinearity rather than any genuine reversal of economic logic. A negative CPI coefficient sitting next to a VIF of 36 is not telling us that inflation depresses coffee prices. It is telling us that OLS cannot separate CPI from the other trending variables it is tangled up with.

The Robusta table is harder to read. WTI, Sugar and Consumption are significant with the expected signs, and COT net MM is again positive and significant, which is reassuring. But several other significant coefficients point in the wrong direction. CPI is negative and significant, DXY is positive and significant, Cocoa is negative and significant. These are not small numerical accidents. They are real reversals that need an explanation, and the most honest one is that 153 training observations and a VIF above 20 for CPI is simply too much collinearity for OLS to handle. The estimator ends up distributing explanatory power across correlated predictors in an arbitrary way, and the signs that come out the other end cannot be trusted as structural parameters.

What both tables are really saying, when read together, is that MLR is not the right tool for this predictor set. Not because the variables are uninformative, but because OLS needs them to be separable, and they are not. The machine learning models that follow are better equipped for exactly this situation, since they do not need to isolate individual effects to produce accurate forecasts.

4.2 ARIMAX

This chunk estimates the ARIMAX model for both coffee series using a walk-forward expanding window. At each step, auto.arima() selects the optimal \((p,d,q)\) order by minimising AIC over the current training window, then generates a one-step-ahead forecast using the next row of exogenous regressors. The model is therefore re-specified at every forecast origin, allowing the autoregressive structure to adapt as new observations are added to the training window. As with the MLR function above, the code is written as a sequence of explicit, separate steps.

Show code 
library(forecast)

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ARIMAX ESTIMATION FUNCTION
#
# Arguments:
#   df      : levels dataset (one row per month)
#   var_dep : name of the dependent variable column
#             ("arabica_price" or "robusta_price")
#   n_train : size of the initial training window (number of
#             rows), computed earlier in the preprocessing chunk
#
# What the function returns:
#   actual    : the observed prices in the test period
#   predicted : the walk-forward one-step-ahead forecasts
#   model     : the ARIMAX model fitted once on the initial
#               training set only (used later for reporting
#               the selected order, coefficients, and residuals)
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_arimax <- function(df, var_dep, n_train) {

  # STEP 1 — Separate the dependent variable from the
  # exogenous regressors. auto.arima() requires the regressors
  # as a plain numeric matrix, not a data frame.
  serie_dependante    <- df[[var_dep]]
  matrice_regresseurs <- as.matrix(df[, vars_exo])

  # Safety check: drop any regressor column that is entirely
  # NA (this should not normally happen, since rows with any
  # NA were already removed upstream by preparer_niveaux()).
  colonnes_valides    <- apply(matrice_regresseurs, 2,
                               function(col) !all(is.na(col)))
  matrice_regresseurs <- matrice_regresseurs[, colonnes_valides, drop = FALSE]

  # STEP 2 — Split into the initial training set and the test
  # set, using the row count computed in the preprocessing chunk.
  n_total <- length(serie_dependante)

  y_train    <- serie_dependante[1:n_train]
  y_test     <- serie_dependante[(n_train + 1):n_total]

  xreg_train <- matrice_regresseurs[1:n_train, ]
  xreg_test  <- matrice_regresseurs[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]

  n_test <- length(y_test)

  # STEP 3 — Walk-forward loop.
  # At forecasting step i, auto.arima() is re-estimated on ALL
  # observations available up to that point: the initial
  # training set, plus every test-period observation already
  # passed (rows 1 to i-1 of y_test / xreg_test). The order
  # (p, d, q) is re-selected by AIC at every step — it is not
  # fixed in advance. The freshly estimated model then produces
  # a single one-step-ahead forecast for observation i, using
  # row i of xreg_test as the future regressor values.
  #
  # Search constraints passed to auto.arima():
  #   max.p = 3, max.q = 3 : keeps the search computationally
  #     feasible across the ~43 re-estimations of the loop
  #   max.d = 1            : consistent with the integration
  #     order established in the stationarity tests
  #   stepwise = TRUE, approximation = TRUE : faster greedy
  #     search instead of an exhaustive grid, needed because
  #     the model is re-estimated at every single step
  #
  # tryCatch() catches any estimation failure (which can happen
  # at the very first steps, when the window is still small)
  # and records NA for that step instead of stopping the loop.
  predictions <- numeric(n_test)

  for (i in 1:n_test) {

    nb_observations_vues <- i - 1   # 0 at step 1, 1 at step 2, ...

    # Observations of the test period already "seen" before step i
    indices_vus <- seq_len(nb_observations_vues)
    y_vu        <- y_test[indices_vus]
    xreg_vu     <- xreg_test[indices_vus, , drop = FALSE]

    # The expanding training window for this step
    y_fenetre    <- c(y_train, y_vu)
    xreg_fenetre <- rbind(xreg_train, xreg_vu)

    modele_arima <- tryCatch(
      auto.arima(y_fenetre, xreg = xreg_fenetre,
                 stepwise      = TRUE,
                 approximation = TRUE,
                 max.p = 3, max.q = 3, max.d = 1),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )

    if (is.null(modele_arima)) {
      predictions[i] <- NA
      next
    }

    # One-step-ahead forecast using row i of the test regressors
    ligne_regresseurs_futurs <- matrix(xreg_test[i, ], nrow = 1)
    prevision <- forecast(modele_arima, h = 1,
                          xreg = ligne_regresseurs_futurs)
    predictions[i] <- prevision$mean[1]
  }

  # STEP 4 — Fit one additional model on the initial training
  # set only (not the walk-forward loop). This single model is
  # kept purely for reporting purposes later in the document:
  # the selected ARIMA order, the regression coefficients, and
  # the residual diagnostics all refer to this training-set-only
  # model rather than to any of the ~43 models re-estimated
  # during the walk-forward loop above.
  modele_sur_entrainement <- auto.arima(y_train, xreg = xreg_train,
                                        stepwise      = TRUE,
                                        approximation = TRUE)

  list(actual    = y_test,
       predicted = predictions,
       model     = modele_sur_entrainement)
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ESTIMATION — ARABICA AND ROBUSTA
# Both series use their respective levels datasets and
# pre-computed training set sizes from the preprocessing chunk.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

res_arimax_ara <- fit_arimax(df_arabica_levels, "arabica_price", n_train_ara_lev)
res_arimax_rob <- fit_arimax(df_robusta_levels, "robusta_price", n_train_rob_lev)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PERFORMANCE METRICS
# calculer_metriques() is applied to the walk-forward
# predictions accumulated over the full test period. Results
# are stored in the same standardised format as the other five
# models for direct combination in the comparative performance
# chunk later in this document.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

metriques_arimax <- rbind(
  cbind(Model = "ARIMAX", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_arimax_ara$actual, res_arimax_ara$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "ARIMAX", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_arimax_rob$actual, res_arimax_rob$predicted))
)

The ARIMAX model delivers strong out-of-sample performance on both series. For Arabica, the model achieves an \(R^2\) of 0.821, with an MSE of 0.029 and an MAE of 0.131 USD/lb, indicating that it captures the broad price dynamics well over the test period. For Robusta, performance is even higher, with an \(R^2\) of 0.929, an MSE of 11,194 and an MAE of 88.7 USD/tonne, confirming that the autoregressive structure of the model, combined with the exogenous variables, explains the vast majority of price variation in the test window. The order \((p,d,q)\) selected by auto.arima() at each walk-forward step varied across iterations, reflecting the adaptive nature of the estimation procedure.

On the full training set, auto.arima() selected a Regression with ARIMA(1,0,0) errors for Arabica and a Regression with ARIMA(3,0,1) errors for Robusta. The absence of differencing (\(d=0\)) in both cases reflects the fact that the trending co-movement between prices and the exogenous regressors is absorbed by the regression component, leaving residuals that are modelled as a stationary autoregressive process. The AR(1) coefficient of 0.967 for Arabica confirms the high degree of price persistence documented in the descriptive analysis. For Robusta, the more complex ARMA(3,1) error structure captures the additional short-run dynamics characteristic of this more volatile series.

The tables below report the regression coefficients of the exogenous regressors from the final ARIMAX model estimated on the full training set for each coffee variety. These coefficients reflect the static linear relationship between each predictor and the dependent price series, conditional on the autoregressive error structure selected by auto.arima(). Two important caveats apply to their interpretation. First, the coefficients are estimated on the training set only and do not incorporate the walk-forward updating that drives the out-of-sample forecasts; they should therefore be read as descriptive of the average relationship over the training period rather than as stable structural parameters. Second, the presence of high multicollinearity among the predictors, documented in the correlation and PCA analyses, implies that individual coefficient estimates and their standard errors may be unstable, and that statistical insignificance of a given regressor does not preclude its contribution to forecast accuracy when combined with other variables.

Show code 
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ARIMAX COEFFICIENT TABLES — ARABICA AND ROBUSTA
# coef() and vcov() extract the regression coefficients and
# their variance-covariance matrix from the final ARIMAX model
# fitted on the full training set. t-statistics and p-values
# are computed manually since forecast objects do not have a
# native tidy() method that separates ARMA from xreg terms.
# Only the exogenous regressor coefficients are displayed —
# the ARMA error structure terms (ar1, ma1, etc.) are excluded
# to focus on the interpretable predictors.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

extraire_coefs_arimax <- function(model, caption_text) {

  co    <- coef(model)
  se    <- sqrt(diag(vcov(model)))
  tstat <- co / se
  pval  <- 2 * pnorm(abs(tstat), lower.tail = FALSE)

  df_coef <- data.frame(
    Variable  = names(co),
    Estimate  = round(co,    4),
    Std_Error = round(se,    4),
    t_stat    = round(tstat, 3),
    P_value   = round(pval,  4),
    Sig       = case_when(
      pval < 0.001 ~ "***",
      pval < 0.01  ~ "**",
      pval < 0.05  ~ "*",
      pval < 0.1   ~ ".",
      TRUE         ~ ""
    ),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ) %>%
  # Keep only exogenous regressors — exclude ARMA terms
  filter(!grepl("^ar|^ma|^intercept|drift", Variable,
                ignore.case = TRUE))

  kable(df_coef,
        caption   = caption_text,
        booktabs  = TRUE,
        row.names = FALSE,
        col.names = c("Variable", "Estimate", "Std. Error",
                      "t-stat", "p-value", "")) %>%
    kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                  font_size = 11, full_width = TRUE)
}

extraire_coefs_arimax(
  res_arimax_ara$model,
  "ARIMAX regression coefficients — Arabica (full training set)"
)

The coefficient tables confirm and sharpen the picture that emerged from the variable importance analysis. For Arabica, only two regressors reach conventional significance thresholds on the full training set: Sugar No.11 prices (\(p < 0.001\)) and WTI crude oil (\(p < 0.01\)). The Sugar coefficient of 1.022 implies that a one-unit increase in the Sugar No.11 price is associated with an increase of approximately USD 1.02/lb in the Arabica futures price. The positive WTI coefficient is consistent with the energy cost channel. The remaining regressors, including the USDA fundamentals, climate indices and the COT net position, are individually insignificant in the static regression, despite contributing meaningfully to out-of-sample forecasting accuracy in the machine learning models. This apparent contradiction may reflect the high multicollinearity among predictors documented in the correlation and PCA analyses: individually insignificant regressors can collectively carry predictive information that the ensemble methods exploit through non-linear combinations.

For Robusta, CPI (\(p < 0.01\)) and WTI (\(p < 0.05\)) are significant, confirming the dominant role of macroeconomic conditions in this market. The COT net Managed Money position is highly significant (\(p < 0.001\)) with a positive coefficient of 0.003, indicating that each additional net long contract held by speculative funds is associated with a USD 0.003/tonne increase in the Robusta futures price, a small per-contract effect that becomes economically meaningful at the scale of tens of thousands of contracts documented in the descriptive analysis. The USDA fundamentals remain individually insignificant for Robusta as well, for the same multicollinearity reasons as Arabica.

Before interpreting these coefficients, it is worth asking whether the model can even identify individual effects reliably given the degree of correlation among the predictors.

This chunk computes the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) for each of the 14 exogenous regressors included in the ARIMAX model, separately for Arabica and Robusta. VIF is computed on an equivalent OLS model estimated on the initial training window, which is the standard approach since the vif() function from the car package operates on lm() objects. The ARMA error structure of ARIMAX does not affect the collinearity structure of the regressors, so the VIF values are directly interpretable in the ARIMAX context. Variables with a VIF above 10 are highlighted in red and classified as severe; variables between 5 and 10 are highlighted in orange and classified as moderate. This diagnostic provides a formal quantification of the multicollinearity already suggested by the correlation matrix and PCA analyses, and offers a structural explanation for the low number of individually significant coefficients observed in the tables above.

Show code 
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# VARIANCE INFLATION FACTORS — ARIMAX REGRESSORS
# The coefficient tables above show that few regressors reach
# conventional significance thresholds in either ARIMAX model.
# One plausible explanation is severe multicollinearity among
# the 14 predictors, already suggested by the correlation
# matrix and PCA analyses. The Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)
# quantifies this formally: for each regressor, it measures
# how much its variance is inflated relative to what it would
# be if it were orthogonal to all other predictors.
#
# VIF interpretation thresholds:
#   VIF < 5      : acceptable
#   5 ≤ VIF < 10 : moderate multicollinearity
#   VIF ≥ 10     : severe — coefficient estimates and standard
#                  errors are unreliable
#
# VIF is computed on an equivalent OLS model estimated on the
# initial training window. This is the standard approach since
# vif() from the car package operates on lm() objects. The
# ARMA error structure of ARIMAX does not affect the regressor
# collinearity structure, so the VIF values are directly
# interpretable in the ARIMAX context.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

library(car)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# DISPLAY LABELS
# Internal variable names are replaced with the same readable
# English labels used in the correlation matrix and PCA plots,
# ensuring visual consistency across all figures in the document.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

labels_vif <- c(
  "sugar_price"    = "Sugar",
  "cocoa_price"    = "Cocoa",
  "cpi"            = "CPI",
  "wti"            = "WTI",
  "fed_funds_rate" = "Fed Funds Rate",
  "dxy"            = "DXY",
  "production"     = "Production",
  "consumption"    = "Consumption",
  "exports"        = "Exports",
  "ending_stocks"  = "Ending stocks",
  "indice_precip"  = "Precipitation",
  "indice_temp"    = "Temperature",
  "oni"            = "ONI",
  "cot_net_mm"     = "COT net MM"
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# REUSABLE VIF FUNCTION
# Encapsulates the lm() estimation, vif() computation and
# kableExtra rendering in a single call. Avoids duplicating
# the same block for Arabica and Robusta.
#
# Arguments:
#   df_levels      : levels dataset (complete cases only)
#   var_dep        : name of the dependent variable column
#   n_train        : size of the initial training window
#   couleur_header : hex colour for the table header row
#   caption_text   : caption string passed to kable()
# ----------------------------------------------------------

calculer_vif <- function(df_levels, var_dep, n_train,
                         couleur_header, caption_text) {

  # Fit the equivalent OLS model on the training window.
  # as.formula() constructs the formula dynamically so the
  # function works with any dependent variable name.
  modele_lm <- lm(
    as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ .")),
    data = df_levels[1:n_train, c(var_dep, vars_exo)]
  )

  vif_scores <- vif(modele_lm)

  # Replace internal names with display labels
  names(vif_scores) <- labels_vif[names(vif_scores)]

  # Build the display data frame with a diagnostic column
  # so the severity interpretation is explicit in the table
  # rather than conveyed only through row colour.
  df_vif <- data.frame(
    Variable   = names(vif_scores),
    VIF        = round(vif_scores, 2),
    Diagnostic = case_when(
      vif_scores >= 10 ~ "Severe",
      vif_scores >=  5 ~ "Moderate",
      TRUE             ~ "Acceptable"
    ),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )

  # Colour vectors for text and background of Diagnostic cell,
  # applied row by row via column_spec() below.
  text_colors <- case_when(
    vif_scores >= 10 ~ "#c0392b",
    vif_scores >=  5 ~ "#d35400",
    TRUE             ~ "#27ae60"
  )

  bg_colors <- case_when(
    vif_scores >= 10 ~ "#fdf2f2",
    vif_scores >=  5 ~ "#fef6ec",
    TRUE             ~ "#f2faf5"
  )

  kable(df_vif,
        caption   = caption_text,
        booktabs  = TRUE,
        row.names = FALSE,
        col.names = c("Variable", "VIF", "Diagnostic")) %>%
    kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                  font_size = 11, full_width = FALSE) %>%
    # Colour the VIF value in red/orange for severe/moderate cases
    column_spec(2,
                bold  = vif_scores >= 5,
                color = ifelse(vif_scores >= 10, "#c0392b",
                        ifelse(vif_scores >=  5, "#d35400",
                               "black"))) %>%
    # Colour the Diagnostic cell background and text
    column_spec(3,
                bold       = vif_scores >= 5,
                color      = text_colors,
                background = bg_colors) %>%
    row_spec(0, bold = TRUE,
             background = couleur_header, color = "white")
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ARABICA VIF
# Training window: n_train_ara_lev rows (2006-06 to end of
# training period), the same window used by fit_arimax().
# ----------------------------------------------------------

calculer_vif(
  df_levels      = df_arabica_levels,
  var_dep        = "arabica_price",
  n_train        = n_train_ara_lev,
  couleur_header = "#8B4513",
  caption_text   = "Variance Inflation Factors — Arabica ARIMAX regressors (training set)"
)
